Nothing metaphysical or physical, nothing supernatural or natural can be discussed without the principle of causation. It is self-evident (and this will be demonstrated below) that there are four kinds of causation, as understood by the classical definition[4]. These types of causation are:

  • material causation
  • efficient causation
  • formal causation
  • final causation

Recall that causation is the CAUSE or REASON for any EFFECT—the necessary "BECAUSE" for every consequence. This also happens to correspond with the being of the effect or subject—the answer to the "what is?" query.

Material causation concerns, obviously, the matter of the effect or subject. A marble statue is a marble statue BECAUSE it is made of marble, BECAUSE its matter is marble. This is the material cause.

The efficient cause is that which is generally understood by people when "cause" is referenced; the efficient cause of the fourth domino in a chain falling is the third domino, which fell on it. The efficient cause is that which moves something to its effect. To again cite the statue example, the efficient cause would be the chisel that moulds it into its form; the marble statue is a marble statue BECAUSE it was chiselled to be so.

The formal cause (asserted by Aristotle to be the most important[4]) is the form or idea (ideal) after which the effect is modelled. With our statue, the formal cause is the idea in the sculptor's mind prior to and throughout the sculpting; the marble statue is a marble statue BECAUSE the sculptor had a vision of the statue when first perceiving the block of marble and setting out to transform that marble into a statue. Worth noting when considering this type of causation is Plato's theory of the "realm of forms"[5], a kind of heaven where there exists a perfect "form" of every "thing", after which every thing (every table, chair, rock, tree, and even person) is modelled. This was Plato's primitive attempt to visualize the mind of God.

The final cause is the "why", the purpose for which any effect is caused. The final cause is the telos—the end. Our statue came to be BECAUSE the sculptor (or whoever hired him) wanted to emulate some person or character, wanted to glorify some personage, and so the marble became a statue.

Note that if any of these four causes had been absent, the marble statue would not have come to be, the effect would not have occurred.

This logically applies to every conceivable effect. If an effect lacks substance (material cause), it cannot be. If it lacks a mover (efficient cause), it cannot be moved. If it lacks a form (formal cause), it cannot exist (how can a table be a table, or an asteroid an asteroid, if the form or idea of table or asteroid does not exist? Quantum mechanics validates this logic; more on this later). And if an effect lacks a purpose (final cause), it could not exist (for nothing would have driven it to exist).

Note that for the formal and final causes, the immediately preceding domino need not be the source of the form or the telos, but somewhere earlier in the chain these causes must exist (whoever pushed over the first domino). These causes also cannot simply be dismissed by an appeal to "accidents" because it was still a cause that set whatever effects in motion, and all actions, all causes, require all four types of causation, or else are consequent from all four types of causation. Otherwise there never would have been any effects.

Recall the five demonstrations of St. Thomas Aquinas from Treatise 1:

1) there has to be a first mover not moved by anything, a being that is non-physical, pure act;

2) there must be a first efficient cause, a being whose essence is existence;

3) there must be an absolutely necessary being;

4) there must exist a wholly good, wholly perfect being; and

5) there must be an intelligent being that conducts all things in nature.

The first proof is simply a statement of the necessity of causation for anything to be. All things observable change, and are moved; in other words there are effects, and these require causes. This is the essential principle of causation we began with. An infinite regression of causality is impossible (even if the universe were infinite and eternal this would be inconceivable, but the universe is not infinite or eternal), and so there must be a first cause, a Prima Causa—a God.

The second proof is an explicit statement of efficient causation. An effect cannot cause itself (so says the principle of causation that we must accept to even discuss this topic), and efficient causes cannot infinitely regress, thus there must be a first efficient cause.

The third proof is a statement of material cause: contingent things do not have "the beginning of existence in themselves", i.e. even the matter that makes a thing itself has a cause, and this, too, cannot infinitely regress; there must be an absolutely necessary being, whose existence is not contingent upon anything else. This also ties into the quantum mechanics proof to be discussed later.

The fouth proof is a statement of formal cause: this depends on value, and acknowledges that things (effects) are imperfect insofar as they must originate from something of greater perfection than themselves (since perfection cannot come from imperfection, or a lesser imperfection from a greater imperfection; that which is more perfect can only come from that which is even more perfect, be this a single source or a sum of sources). The fifth proof is a statement of final cause. Since all effects must move towards a purpose (or else they never would have become part of a causal chain), and since unconscious things cannot move themselves willingly toward their purpose, such effects must be moved by an intelligent being in order to aim at telos. A hierarchy of more intelligent beings ad infinitum is logically absurd; therefore there must be an intelligent being that conducts all things in nature.

In order to demonstrate the untenability of atheism and materialism, we must be clear on what these terms mean.

"Atheism" derives from the Greek θεός, meaning "God", and the Greek prefix α-, meaning "not" or "without"; literally "without God". From the outset atheism is a negation, a denial, and posits that the universe exists and came about without a God. But what is meant by "God"?

Different people will have different understandings (and later it will be shown that only one understanding is true), but few will disagree that God is understood to be the supreme, omnipotent being who is both Creator and Ruler of the entire universe (read: of everything). Atheism rejects the existence of such a being.

Materialism is even more easily understood: the view that all things are reducible to matter. Webster's has defined materialism as the "doctrine of materialists" and a materialist as "One who denies the existence of spiritual substances, and maintains that the soul of man is the result of a particular organization of matter in the body."[8] A materialist might object to this and assert that there is no soul that matter need comprise, but this only displays a lack of understanding of the classical notion of the soul and all that it has been used to describe. Obviously the materialist rejects the soul as a spiritual entity; that is included in the first part of the definition. What the second part of the definition explains is that free will, consciousness, and morality—all of which are classically explained by the soul—must be explained in material terms by the materialist, or else rejected also. In the words of Thomas Nagel, "Materialism is the view that only the physical world is irreducibly real, and a place must be found in it for mind, if there is such a thing."[9]

Atheism and materialism, then, are effectively the same in that both reject the existence of the spiritual and maintain that all things can be explained in material terms alone.

Now, it is often asserted that atheism / materialism is the "default", that theists are required to prove their theories but the atheists, being "the default", are not. This of course is absurd; atheists are as much making a negative claim as the theists are making a positive claim, and both types of claims place the burden of proof on the one making the claim. The atheists try to escape this burden of proof by shifting it onto the theist, but they can only do so by committing the argument from ignorance fallacy, by assuming the theist proposition to be false simply because it has not been proven to be true! But recall, we already demonstrated in Treatise 1 that no metaphysical theory can be proven to be true; a placement of faith is always necessary!

An argument such as a proof of impossibility is necessary in order to prove the materialist claim, and Treatise 2 demonstrated that this cannot be done, that such attempts inevitably fail, because, in the case of the Hawking argument, the materialist has to assume that his theory is correct in order to use it to "prove" the impossibility of God (and therefore justify materialism)!

While the Natural Law will be discussed later on, it is worth taking a moment to demonstrate a glaring contradiction that emerges for the Enlightenment thinker / materialist as a consequence of rejecting the second point of the Natural Law, namely that nature is intelligible. The materialist might claim that this is not rejected, and yet materialism, by denying the immaterial, is forced to deny anything that cannot be perceived by the senses. Be it called "corpuscular reductionism" or simply "atomism", the materialist attempts to reduce all things to matter, and even if we pretend that the materialist is not at a loss to explain consciousness and the like (see below), it is inconceivable that something like universal meaning or universal order could be reduced to matter...and therefore the universe must be beyond understanding! For, what would there be to measure if there were no immaterial mathematical truths[14]?

We can now move to the failures of atheism / materialism to explain reality. Most troublesome for the materialist is Man, for it is in Man we find the classical understanding of the spirit most thoroughly applied. Specifically, materialism seriously struggles with Consciousness, Cognition, and Value.

The Enlightenment launched the system of belief that all things can be explained in physical terms, and all modern materialists have been struggling to successfully apply such physical theories to the mind ever since. Analytic behaviourism was tried initially, where mental states were reduced to the observable behaviour they produce—an essentially "verificationist" strategy[10], asserting that all that is required to describe a mental state is to describe the behavioural effects an observer can perceive. Obviously this says nothing about the fundamental issue: the actual subjective experience of the one whose mental state is being studied.

So it was that nonanalytic attempts began, and these are those generally accepted (read: assumed to be sufficient) by materialists today, despite their unresolved flaws. Specifically, that mental events (Ψ) are physical events (Φ) in the brain, Ψ = Φ[11]. In other words, a mental event such as the taste of sugar or the pain of being stabbed is the corresponding physical event in the central nervous system (electrical signals, firing neurons, and chemical reactions). This is not a conceptual theory because it cannot be known a priori. This is a scientific theory, which can only be known a posteriori, as much as Water = H2O might have been a theory before being validated by scientific testing[11].

The unresolved question, of course, is "What is it about Φ that makes it also Ψ? It must be some property conceptually distinct from the physical properties that define Φ. That is required for the identity to be a scientific and not a conceptual truth"[11] (see above). Unlike theism, which does not reject the immaterial aspect of the universe (and therefore half of the types of causation, which are self-evidently real as long as anything exists, see Treatise 2), materialism as a theory cannot explain consciousness.

Cognition is another hurdle for the materialists. Even animals are conscious, but now we hone in specifically on humanity with cognition and the ability to reason, which is troublesome for reasons beyond just those of explaining consciousness, which is a prerequisite for cognition[12].

To reason is, in part, to be able to make judgments about objective reality independent of what our senses reveal. In nature we may never perceive four identical apples, and so we could not in nature make an abstract judgment such as "two apples plus two apples always yield four", for this abstract judgment depends on a theoretical apple that is always equivalent to other apples, a form, in the Platonic sense, that transcends material reality. The fact that human beings can conceive of such forms, such transcendent ideals; the fact that we can develop abstractions such as mathematics, which are purely ideal, and apply them successfully to the far from ideal material reality, is not something that materialists are any better equipped to explain than consciousness. True, material phenomena can be related to such thoughts, such cognition, but as the theories exist today they are insufficient for actually explaining these phenomena (and all signs indicate that they will remain inadequate).
